transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Um… hi, Dr. Smith. I guess my work got worried about me. I’m a waitress, and lately during service I’ve been kind of… getting stuck, I guess. Like I’ll freeze in the middle of doing something, or I’ll do things in the wrong order.

It probably looked worse than it was, but one time I was standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key, just repeating table numbers instead of closing out checks. Everyone got scared, and I felt really embarrassed. I’m not trying to cause problems or anything… I just thought I should come in and talk to someone.
During that episode at the soda station, do you remember what was happening around you, or is there a gap in your memory for that time?

I don’t think it was a total blank, no… I remember being there. I remember the soda station, and I had the cash drawer key in my hand, which I know probably sounds strange.

It’s more like I got stuck, not like I disappeared. I wasn’t closing out the checks the way I was supposed to—I was just sort of repeating the table numbers, like I was trying to organize it in my head but couldn’t get to the next step. I’m sorry, that probably doesn’t explain it very well.
About how long did that episode at the soda station last, from when you first felt stuck until you felt back to normal?

Um… I’m not totally sure. It felt longer to everyone else than it did to me, I think. Maybe a few minutes? Long enough that people noticed I wasn’t moving on—like I was just standing there with the key and saying the table numbers instead of closing the checks.

I did come back to myself after that, though. I mean, I wasn’t trying to be difficult or anything. Does that answer what you mean?
Has anything like this happened before this incident at work, or was this the first time you noticed this kind of 'stuck' episode?

It wasn’t exactly the first time, no. I mean… I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but there had been smaller moments before where I’d sort of freeze during service or get the order of things mixed up.

The soda station thing was just the one that really scared people, I think—because I was standing there holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers instead of closing the checks like I was supposed to. Before that, I guess I’d noticed little versions of it, but I tried to brush them off. Does that make sense?

During these episodes, did anyone notice your body becoming stiff or rigid, or did they have to move your arms or body into a position that you then held, like your muscles resisted or stayed frozen in place?

I don’t think anyone had to, like, move my arms into a position or anything like that. Not that I know of.

What they noticed was more that I was freezing up in the middle of service, or doing things in the wrong order. Like with the soda station, I was just standing there holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers instead of closing checks. So it was more… stuck in what I was doing, I guess, not someone having to physically reposition me. Does that answer it?
During these episodes, did anyone notice you making any repetitive movements—like lip-smacking, chewing motions, or fumbling with your clothes or objects—that you weren't aware of at the time?

I don’t remember anyone saying I was doing things like lip-smacking or chewing, no. If I was fumbling with something, it was more like… I had the cash drawer key in my hand and I just wasn’t moving on to the next step.

What scared everyone was that I kind of froze in the middle of service, or did things out of order—like standing by the soda station repeating table numbers instead of closing the checks. I wasn’t trying to be odd or anything. That’s the part they noticed, I think.
Right after one of these episodes ends, do you feel confused, unusually tired, or foggy for a while afterward, or do you feel back to your normal self almost right away?

I guess I wouldn’t say I snap back right away, exactly… but it’s hard to explain. Mostly I feel embarrassed and kind of shaken once I realize people were watching or that I messed up the flow.

Like, with the soda station thing, what scared everyone was that I was just standing there holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers instead of closing the checks. Afterward I knew that wasn’t what I was supposed to be doing, but I was more… trying to act normal and catch up, I think. I don’t want to overstate it. Does that answer what you mean by foggy?
Have any of these episodes ever happened when you were relaxed, alone, or even asleep, or do they only seem to occur during busy, stressful moments at work?

As far as I know, it’s really been during the busy work moments. Like when service is backed up and there are a lot of things happening at once.

I haven’t had someone tell me it happened while I was asleep or anything, and I don’t think it’s happened just relaxing alone. The times people got scared were at work—me kind of freezing up mid-service or doing things out of order, like standing by the soda station with the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers instead of closing checks. It sounds worse when I say it like that, but… yeah, it seems tied to those stressful moments.
Right before one of these episodes begins, do you ever notice any unusual warning signs—like a strange smell or taste, a wave of fear, a feeling of déjà vu, or a rising sensation in your stomach?

I don’t think so… not like a clear warning sign. I haven’t noticed a strange smell or taste, or that déjà vu feeling you mentioned.

Maybe I get tense because it’s busy, but that feels more like normal work stress than some specific signal beforehand. I’m sorry, I know that’s probably not very helpful. I just don’t remember anything unusual right before it starts.

During one of these episodes, if a coworker called your name loudly or touched your arm, would that ever snap you out of it or get your attention, or do you stay completely unresponsive until it passes on its own?

I think… if they say my name loud enough, sometimes I kind of notice, but I don’t always respond right away. It’s not like I’m trying to ignore them.

What people at work told me is more that I sort of freeze in the middle of service, or I start doing the wrong thing in the wrong order. Like that time by the soda station—I was just standing there with the cash drawer key, repeating table numbers instead of closing checks. I’m embarrassed saying it, because it sounds dramatic, but that’s what scared them. I don’t know if someone touching my arm would fully snap me out of it, exactly.

Have you ever had any of these episodes turn into shaking, jerking movements, loss of bladder control, or biting your tongue, or has a doctor ever told you that you have epilepsy or another seizure disorder?

No… I don’t think so. Nobody’s ever told me I was shaking or jerking, and I haven’t had, like, bladder accidents or bitten my tongue that I know of.

And no doctor has told me I have epilepsy or a seizure disorder. I mean, unless there’s something I’m not understanding, but as far as I know, no.

No… I don’t think so. Nobody’s ever told me I was shaking or jerking, and I haven’t had, like, bladder accidents or bitten my tongue that I know of.

And no doctor has told me I have epilepsy or a seizure disorder. I mean, unless there’s something I’m not understanding, but as far as I know, no.

inference.note: Absence of postictal confusion, automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing), tongue biting, incontinence, or convulsive movements, and episodes occurring only during stress rather than randomly or during sleep, make epileptic seizure (G40.9) unlikely. Findings are more consistent with stress-triggered dissociative episodes.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit and the chief complaint
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with recurrent episodes of psychomotor 'freezing' and disorganized behavior sequencing (e.g., holding cash drawer key while repetitively stating table numbers instead of closing checks) occurring specifically during high-stress work periods. These episodes are brief (minutes), retain partial environmental awareness (not full unresponsiveness), lack a prodromal aura, lack post-ictal confusion, lack automatisms (no lip-smacking, chewing), lack motor rigidity/catalepsy requiring repositioning, and lack convulsive activity, tongue-biting, or incontinence. No history of epilepsy. The clinical picture—episodic disruption of normal integration of movement/behavior triggered by psychological stress, inconsistent with a defined neurological or seizure pattern—is most consistent with a functional neurological/dissociative-type symptom presentation not fitting classic conversion (motor/sensory loss) or specific dissociative subtypes, thus best captured as Other dissociative and conversion disorders (F44.89).
